newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. promises to help Taiwan's WTO bid - radio.
newsitem.headline: U.S. promises to help Taiwan's WTO bid - radio.

text.p: The United States has promised to help Taiwan's bid to enter the World Trade Organisation as the sides began a rare senior-level meeting on Monday, Taiwan's economics minister was quoted on Monday as saying.
"The U.S. side has promised to help our country to enter the World Trade Organisation as soon as possible," state-run radio quoted Economics Minister Wang Chih-kang as saying.
Wang made the comment after meeting with U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers before the sides started a one-day economic dialogue on Monday morning.
Summers and his delegation were scheduled to meet economics vice minister Hsu Ke-sheng and other economic and foreign affairs officials during the talks.
"The U.S. side also hopes to hold further talks about exchanges of high-level official visits and on investment obstacles as soon as possible," Wang was quoted as saying.
Washington switched diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei in 1979 but keeps close trade ties with the island.

Taiwan officials have warned it could be difficult for the diplomatically isolated island to join the WTO if Beijing were allowed to join first, and urged the world trade body not to be swayed by China's political agenda when considering its entry.
China, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war separated them in 1949, says the island is not entitled to membership as a sovereign in international bodies.

Beijing has said it would accept Taiwan's membership as a customs territory, but not before China itself is allowed to join the world trade club. Western powers have cited China's market barriers in excluding it from the WTO.
Summers is the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit since Transportation Secretary Federico Pena came in December 1994.
"Vice Minister Summers thinks there are still problems in medical equipment (imports), and the economics ministry promises to seek for reasonable solutions," Wang said on the radio.
U.S. medical equipment makers have accused Taiwan of blocking their exports to the island by imposing special requirements on local importers.
"If necessary, we will send a team to the United States to further discuss with them," Wang said.
Taiwan also would try to further open up markets and remove investment obstacles, the radio quoted Wang as saying.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, while China's demand to join GATT by the end of 1994 was rejected.
